clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive congenital enteropathy caused chiefly by biallelic EPCAM variants, with a syndromic form linked to SPINT2
Presents in early infancy with severe watery diarrhoea and failure to thrive requiring parenteral nutrition
Small-bowel biopsy shows villus atrophy, crypt abnormalities and characteristic focal epithelial tufts of crowded, disorganised enterocytes
EpCAM immunostaining is typically reduced or absent at the enterocyte membrane, supporting the diagnosis
The diarrhoea reflects disrupted enterocyte adhesion and impaired absorptive surface rather than a single transporter defect
The SPINT2-related variant may be accompanied by choanal atresia, keratitis and other congenital anomalies
Long-term nutritional dependence is common, and severe refractory cases may require intestinal transplantation
reference.pathophysiology: Tufting enteropathy results from defective enterocyte adhesion and epithelial organisation. Loss-of-function variants in EPCAM disrupt the epithelial cell adhesion molecule, impairing cell-cell contacts and the normal architecture of the intestinal epithelium. Enterocytes crowd and pile into focal tufts at the villus surface, with associated villus atrophy and crypt changes, so the absorptive surface is compromised. The syndromic SPINT2-associated form involves a serine protease inhibitor and additional developmental anomalies. The net effect is failure of fluid and nutrient absorption producing chronic diarrhoea from early infancy.
additionalDifferentials: Coeliac disease and other later-onset enteropathies
additionalInvestigations: Small-bowel mucosal biopsy with assessment for epithelial tufts and villus atrophy
Stool electrolytes and faecal osmotic gap to characterise the diarrhoea
Molecular testing for EPCAM and SPINT2 variants
Assessment for extraintestinal anomalies (e.g. choanal, ophthalmic) in suspected syndromic disease
redFlags: Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance in a young infant with intractable diarrhoea
Failure to thrive despite optimised feeding, indicating a congenital enteropathy
Associated congenital anomalies suggesting the syndromic SPINT2-related form
Complications of long-term parenteral nutrition such as line sepsis or cholestasis
reference.prognosis: Most patients require prolonged or indefinite parenteral nutrition; some achieve partial enteral tolerance while severe refractory disease may progress to intestinal transplantation. Outcome is influenced by nutritional complications and any associated anomalies.
pitfalls: Confusing the histology with coeliac disease or other villus-atrophy enteropathies without recognising the diagnostic tufts
Relying on light microscopy alone rather than adding EpCAM staining and genetics
Attributing chronic diarrhoea to feed intolerance and delaying definitive evaluation
Missing associated congenital anomalies that point to a syndromic cause
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Long-term parenteral nutrition as the mainstay to sustain fluid, electrolyte and nutritional needs from early infancy
Meticulous central venous catheter care with prevention and prompt treatment of catheter-related bloodstream infection and line complications
Cautious introduction and advancement of enteral feeds to promote any achievable enteral tolerance
Monitoring and management of intestinal-failure-associated liver disease, growth, and micronutrient and trace-element status
Consideration of intestinal or combined liver-intestinal transplantation for refractory disease or failure of parenteral nutrition
Assessment and management of associated anomalies (choanal atresia, keratitis) in SPINT2-related syndromic disease
Multidisciplinary intestinal-failure and gastroenterology care, with genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance
